analytic.title: Estimation of Deadline Miss Rate for DAG Mixed Timer-driven and Event-driven Nodes

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Autonomous-driving systems are becoming increasingly complex, making it more difficult to predict timing. Autonomous-driving applications, such as localization and path planning, can be represented by a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) consisting of timer-driven and event-driven nodes. Various estimation methods have been proposed for determining the response time of a DAG. However, most existing studies rely on worstcase execution time estimation, leading to pessimistic results. Additionally, there is a lack of research on DAGs that incorporate a combination of timer-driven and event-driven nodes. To address this issue, a proposed method estimates the response time and deadline miss rates considering the variation in execution time for DAGs with mixed node types. By considering execution time variation, the proposed method allows for multiple values of response time and deadline miss rate based on probability. When a sufficient number of cores are available, the proposed method accurately estimates the deadline miss rate.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In recent years, there has been significant progress in the development of autonomous-driving systems, which are anticipated to make valuable contributions to society. These systems are expected to reduce traffic accidents. However, due to their hardware control nature, autonomous-driving systems are bound by strict deadlines. A deadline represents the time by which the system must complete its processing to ensure valid output. Consequently, it is crucial to design systems that can reliably meet these deadlines. Nevertheless, meeting deadlines is challenging due to the intricate structure of autonomousdriving systems [1].

A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a useful model for representing complex systems. In a DAG, tasks within the system are represented as nodes, while the communication of data between tasks is represented as edges. A DAG facilitates the consideration of methods focused on meeting deadlines, such as scheduling, which considers the order of task execution [2], [3]. An autonomous-driving system can be divided into two types of nodes: timer-driven nodes that activate at periods, and event-driven nodes that activate once input data has been received [4]. In an autonomous-driving system, multiple timerdriven nodes exist at the source and in the middle of the DAG that runs at different periods [5]. While existing studies have proposed scheduling methods for autonomous-driving systems [6]- [8], most of them utilize worst-case execution time (WCET) as the basis for scheduling. WCET represents the longest expected execution time for a given node, often overestimating the actual execution time. The problem with using WCET for scheduling is that it leads to pessimistic scheduling results [9], potentially resulting in deadline misses.

One approach to address the pessimistic results is to express the execution time in terms of probability. By expressing the possible execution times and probabilities taken by each node in a matrix, the execution times of consecutive nodes can be calculated. This allows the derivation of end-to-end response time patterns and probabilities taken and prevents pessimistic estimation. When dealing with DAGs that contain a mixture of timer-driven and event-driven nodes, the analysis of data passing among timer-driven nodes becomes complex [10]. The inclusion of execution time variations further compounds this complexity. The variations in execution time due to probabilistic execution times introduce multiple patterns of data passing to the timer-driven node behind. Consequently, accurately estimating the response time becomes difficult.

This paper proposes an estimation method for the response time and the deadline miss rate using probabilistic execution time. In a DAG without branches to simplify the analysis, the proposed method estimates the response time of the path from source to sink. The path consists of timer-driven nodes at the source and in the middle, and the proposed method needs to predict the number of data instances that will be sent to the timer-driven node upon activation. The response time estimation is based on the results of the predicted data passing. Once the response time is estimated, the method calculates the rate at which each instance of the sink node will miss its deadline. This provides insights into the likelihood of missing deadlines for individual instances. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

• The proposed method identifies data dependencies among timer-driven nodes with varying execution times. • The proposed method addresses the challenge of estimating the path deadline miss rate when the execution time of a node exhibits probabilistic variations. • The proposed method accurately estimates the deadline miss rate when the number of cores is sufficient.

This paper is structured as follows. Section II defines the system model using DAGs and nodes. Section III describes the proposed method of deadline miss rate estimation. Section IV presents an evaluation of the proposed method. Section V presents existing studies related to the proposed method. Section VI summarizes this paper and discusses future work.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The system model used in the proposed method is defined in this section. It covers DAG representation, statistics related to the variation in execution time, and the path. Parameters and functions related to the system model are listed in Table I.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: The target system is represented using a DAG, which comprises nodes and edges. An illustrative example of such a DAG is depicted in Fig. 1. The DAG is denoted as G = (V, E), where V represents a set of nodes and E represents a set of edges. Each node in the DAG represents a specific task within the system. To identify individual nodes, a subscript notation is utilized, such as v i ∈ V .

Nodes start and end connected by edges are defined. A predecessor node is the previous node of two nodes connected by an edge. The function that returns the set of predecessor nodes of a node v is pre(v). Conversely, a successor node is a node behind two nodes connected by an edge. The function that returns the set of successor nodes of a node v is suc(v). In Fig. 1, pre(v 9 ) = {v 2 , v 5 }, and suc(v 9 ) = {v 10 }.

Nodes located at the start and end of the DAG are referred to in the following manner. A source node is a node that does not have any predecessor nodes and is represented by v src ∈ V src . V src denotes the set of source nodes within the DAG. Moreover, a sink node is a node that does not have any successor nodes. It is assumed in this paper that each DAG contains a single sink node. The sink node is denoted as v sink . In Fig. 1, this can be expressed as
div.formula: V src = {v 1 , v 3 , v 6 }, v sink = v 11 .
div.p: Nodes can be categorized into two types based on their activation method: timer-driven nodes and event-driven nodes. The definition of these node types aligns with the studies [11] conducted in the context of autonomous-driving systems.

A timer-driven node is a node that is activated at regular intervals with a consistent period. In the autonomousdriving systems, sensor nodes fall under this category as they continuously gather input from the surrounding environment. Additionally, timer-driven nodes encompass nodes responsible for periodic output to ensure safe driving, such as localization and control. For example, Autoware [12] incorporates an ekf localizer that estimates the position of the vehicle. div.p: Here, c i denotes the execution time, T i represents the period of activation, and φ i indicates the offset, representing the initial activation time.

An event-driven node is a type of node that is activated upon receiving data from its predecessor nodes. When an eventdriven node has multiple predecessor nodes, it becomes activated only after receiving output from all of its predecessors. If a node v i is classified as an event-driven node, it is denoted as v ed i . The set of event-driven nodes is represented as V ed . The event-driven node v ed i has only the execution time c i . In a DAG, edges symbolize the data dependencies between nodes. A data dependency represents the relationship where one node sends data to another node. Therefore, the edge connecting node v i to v j can be represented as e i,j ∈ E.

The execution time of a node exhibits variations within values below the WCET. Consequently, the proposed method addresses the execution time while taking these variations into account. The execution time of a node v i , denoted as c i , is represented as a 2 × k matrix, where k represents the number of varying execution times. This representation is based on the approach described in an existing study [13]. The c i is expressed as follows.

div.p: The first row, c i,j , denotes the execution time taken by node v i . On the other hand, the second row represents the Probabilistic Mass Function (PMF), which describes the probability of each execution time occurring. For instance, the probability that the execution time is c i,1 is denoted as f (c i,1 ). It should be noted that the sum of all probability values in the second row of the matrix is equal to one. The execution time distribution can be derived from statistical analysis of multiple executions of a node. The statistics of crop box filter self, which is the open-source software of autonomous-driving systems, are shown in Fig. 2. The probability is obtained from the overall number of measurements and the number of measurements taking their execution time.

div.head: C. Path
div.p: An end-to-end path is defined to calculate the response time and estimate the deadline miss rate. A path in a DAG is a sequence of nodes connected by edges, and an end-to-end path refers to a path starting from a source node with the largest period and ending at a sink node. This paper focuses on estimating the response time of this end-to-end path.

The node with the largest period is selected as the starting point of the path in order to update the data from all predecessor nodes at each activation. Considering the autonomousdriving system [1], particular attention is given to the response time of the path from the LiDAR to the control module. In this system, the LiDAR is activated at a maximum period of 100 ms.
The end-to-end path π is denoted as follows.
div.formula: π = {vi 1 , vi 2 , • • • , vi n } where {ei j ,i j+1 ∈ E|1 < j < n -1} and vi 1 = maxP eriod(Vsrc) and vi n = vsink
div.p: The end-to-end path is denoted as π = {v 3 , v 4 , v 5 , v 9 , v 10 , v 11 } in Fig. 1. The proposed method also defines length(π) as a function that outputs the number of nodes in the end-to-end path π. In the proposed method, a deadline miss is said to occur when the response time of an end-to-end path exceeds the given deadline.

div.head: III. PROPOSED METHOD
div.p: The rate of deadline misses for an end-to-end path in a DAG is estimated by the proposed method. A deadline miss occurs when the response time of the path exceeds the specified deadline. To explain the proposed method, this section is organized as follows: assumption, overview of the proposed method, chain, data sending/receiving relationships between chains, and the method for estimating the deadline miss rate.

div.head: A. Assumption
div.p: The constraints and assumptions of the system model in dealing with the proposed method are presented. Confluences and branches of the edges of the DAGs and the limitations of the proposed method are described.

Confluences and branches in a DAG make response time estimation difficult. If a node has multiple predecessor nodes, the period of each predecessor node may be different. Different periods make it difficult for a node to estimate when all inputs from multiple predecessor nodes are aligned. The proposed method only focuses on analyzing the data-passing relationship among the timer-driven nodes in a single row. To simplify the analysis, the confluence is made a timer-driven node. As the number of confluences increases with the number of branches, DAGs without branches are targeted.

In this paper, the end-to-end path refers to the path from the source node with the largest period to the sink node in the DAG. If a node that is not part of the end-to-end path is executed first, it has the potential to interfere with the execution of nodes within the end-to-end path. However, as the primary focus of this paper is on the analysis of response time for the end-to-end path, the interference caused by nodes outside of this path is not taken into consideration. Incorporating interference into the response time analysis is an avenue for future work.

The objective of this paper is to estimate the deadline miss rate for a path. Assuming that a deadline is given for a path, a deadline miss is considered when the response time of the path exceeds the deadline.

div.head: B. Overview of Proposed Method
div.p: The proposed method consists of three main steps. The three steps are: 1) dividing the end-to-end path into chains, 2) obtaining data dependencies between chains, and 3) calculating the deadline miss rate from the obtained data dependencies. After three processing steps, the proposed method outputs the deadline miss rate from one DAG.

First, the proposed method divides the end-to-end path into chains. This division is based on grouping consecutive nodes that are activated at the same period. The estimation and analysis of data dependencies become more manageable and straightforward.

Next, the timing of data reception between chains is estimated to analyze the response time. This estimation is crucial for determining when the chain at the source of the DAG can transmit data to the chain at the sink of the DAG. Since the execution time of nodes varies probabilistically, there can be multiple patterns of data reception timings. This paper takes into account these variations and calculates the probabilities associated with each timing pattern.

Finally, the deadline miss rate is calculated based on the information about the timing of data passing from the source chain to the sink chain. Since the sink chain is activated repeatedly within a period, the proposed method checks whether the sink chain meets the deadline for each execution.

div.head: C. Chain
div.p: The end-to-end path may have multiple timer-driven nodes positioned in the middle. These timer-driven nodes play a crucial role in outputting data without being influenced by the sensor period. As timer-driven nodes are activated periodically, the event-driven nodes following them are also activated with a constant period. The reason for this activation pattern is that event-driven nodes are activated by incoming input, while timer-driven nodes output data periodically. To simplify the structure of the DAG and streamline the analysis, the timer-driven node and its successor event-driven nodes, which are activated according to the same period, are collectively referred to as a chain. This grouping makes it easier to analyze data dependencies and estimate response times.

A chain is a sequence of one timer-driven node and its successor event-driven nodes in an end-to-end path. The end of the chain is a sink node or an event-driven node that is the predecessor node of the next timer-driven node. A chain in an end-to-end path π is defined as Γ i , and the chain Γ i is constructed as follows.
div.formula: Γi = {vi 1 , vi 2 , • • • , vi n } where vi 1 ∈ V td and {Γi \ vi 1 } ∈ V ed and Γi ⊂ π

div.head: D. Dependencies of Chains
div.p: Response time analysis requires finding the data dependencies between chains. When there are two consecutive chains, namely Γ i and Γ suc , a waiting interval occurs before the data output by Γ i can be utilized by Γ suc . This is because Γ suc is activated within its period regardless of the availability of the data. The response time is influenced by this waiting time. If the output of Γ i does not arrive in time for Γ suc to use it, the output of Γ i must wait until the next instance of Γ suc is activated. Understanding which instance of Γ suc receives the data from Γ i is essential for accurate response time analysis. The parameters used in this section are described in Table II.

Data dependencies between chains vary with time. This is due to the different periods between chains. To cover the data dependencies, the proposed method performs response time analysis in the hyper-period. The hyper-period is the least common multiple of the period. Depending on the combination of periods, the value of hyper-period may be explosive. However, the 100 ms period of the LiDAR and the 33 ms period of the camera are the causes of the large hyperperiod of the autonomous-driving system [1], and the hyperperiod of the autonomous-driving system can be suppressed to 3, 300 ms.

The data dependencies between chains are determined by considering the variation in execution time. It is possible for a chain instance Γ i to send data to multiple instances of Γ suc . For this purpose, the proposed method uses a matrix to represent the probabilistic index at which the most recent data transfer occurs from Γ i to Γ suc . div.head: E. Deadline Miss Rate Estimation
div.p: The deadline miss rate can be derived from the response time of the path, taking into account the information obtained in Section III-D (pSIN K c (Γ i,j )). In this paper, a deadline miss is defined as occurring when the response time of the endto-end path exceeds the specified deadline. It should be noted that the response time can vary due to two factors. Firstly, the finish time of the sink chain can vary, leading to different response times. Secondly, the index of the sink chain where the data is most recently used may differ, further contributing to variations in the response time.

The deadline miss rate of the path is affected by the variability in the finish time of the sink chain. The response time is determined by the activation time of the source node and the finish time of the sink chain instance. However, since the finish time of the sink chain can vary probabilistically, multiple response times can be obtained. This results in a combination of scenarios where the response time exceeds the deadline (missed deadline) and scenarios where the response time meets the deadline (not missed deadline).

Next, the variation of the deadline miss rate due to the different indexes of the sink chain where the data are most recently used is explained. pSIN K c (Γ i,j ) indicates the index of the sink chain where the data sent from Γ i,j is first used can be known. From pSIN K c (Γ i,j ), the output of one chain instance is used most recently by multiple sink chain instances due to execution time variation. The response time varies because the finish time increases by the sink chain period when the index increases by one.

A method to derive the deadline miss rate is proposed in Algorithm 2. The deadline miss rate differs among sink chain instances because the timing of data arrival differs by period. The parameters used in Algorithm 2 are described in Table III. Algorithm 2 is described below in six steps from 1) to 6). 1) Determine one instance of the sink chain to estimate the deadline miss rate. 2) List up the indexes of the source chain Γ src whose pSIN K(Γ src,src idx ) contains the index of the sink chain determined in 1).

3) For one of the source chain instances listed in 2), calculate the response time from data generation to the finish time of the determined sink chain instance. The reason for calculating the response time for each source chain instance separately is that the data generation time differs depending on the index of the source chain. 4) To derive one miss rate, check whether each response time obtained exceeds the deadline. If the response time from the source chain instance to the determined sink chain instance does not exceed the deadline, one miss rate becomes zero. 5) Calculate the probability of data arrival from the instance of the source chain to the sink chain instance. one miss rate is only valid when the source chain data arrive at the sink chain instance. If the data in the source chain do not reach the sink chain instance, the response time is not generated. arrival rate is derived from pSIN K c (Γ src,src idx ). From the above, the deadline miss rate when data arrives is ) for all instances of the sink chain, the deadline miss rate for each sink chain instance is obtained.

An example of the deadline miss rate estimation method for one sink chain instance is illustrated in Fig. 5. A chain Γ 1 has a period of 100, 35 for 30% of the execution time, and 80 for 70% of the execution time, and a chain Γ 2 has a period of 70, 30 for 80% of the execution time, and 50 for 20% of the execution time. In this explanation, the deadline is set to 80. The proposed method now calculates the deadline miss rate of Γ 2,3 . Deadline misses occur when data arrives from Γ 1,1 (response times are 170 and 190) and when data arrives from Γ 1,2 with a 20% probability (response time is 90). Therefore, one miss rate from Γ 1,1 to Γ 2,3 is 100%, and one miss rate from Γ 1,2 to Γ 2,3 is 20%. The deadline is met when data arrives from Γ 1,2 and when the execution time of Γ 2,3 is 30 (response time is 70). When Γ 2,3 receive data, arrival rate of Γ 1,1 is 100%, and arrival rate of Γ 1,2 is 30%. Therefore, the deadline miss rate instance miss rate when data arrives from Γ 1,1 is 100% (1.0 * 1.0 = 1.0), and instance miss rate when data arrives from Γ 1,2 is 76% (0.3 * 0.2 + 0.7 = 0.76). Combining these deadline miss rates, the deadline miss rate for Γ 2,3 is 76% (1.0 * 0.76 = 0.76).

IV. EVALUATION The accuracy of the proposed method is evaluated in this section. First, the tools and parameters used in the evaluation are described. Next, the estimated and measured deadline miss rates are compared.

div.head: A. Preparation for Evaluation
div.p: Randomly generated DAGs were used to evaluate the proposed method and confirm its generality. The deadline miss rate estimated by the proposed method is compared with the deadline miss rate measured by scheduling nodes with varying execution times. The smaller the difference, the more accurately the deadline miss rate was estimated.

The parameters of the randomly generated DAGs are described below. A total of 600 DAGs were generated using the random DAG generation tool RD-Gen [11]. The number of nodes takes values from 10 to 80. The period takes values from 10 to 100 in increments of 10. The maximum number of nodes and periods are based on the autonomous-driving system [1]. The maximum period refers to LiDAR, which is the maximum period for the autonomous-driving system. The utilization of the DAG is varied between 0.5 and 0.75. The reason for not keeping the utilization rate closer to one is that the DAGs are not targeted at DAGs where deadline misses occur frequently.

The proposed method estimates response times for models with varying execution times. The distribution of execution times of the nodes is treated as a normal distribution, and the maximum of the distribution is equal to the WCET. The probabilistic execution time c i of each node is constructed as a 2 × 5 matrix as in Eq. ( 1) and shall take five values below WCET based on the distribution of execution times. The larger the number of columns in the matrix of node execution times, the more complex the proposed method becomes to calculate, and the number of columns is limited to five. The deadline is set as the response time when all nodes continue to take a value between WCET and one step less execution time.

The measured deadline miss rate calculation is based on simulations. In the simulation, each node randomly adopts one of the five execution times. The simulation is performed 200 times, and the percentage is calculated from the number of deadline misses in the simulation. In the simulation, priority is given to the node with the earliest tentative start time.

div.head: B. Evaluation of Deadline Miss Rate Estimation
div.p: The evaluation is based on the difference between the estimated deadline miss rate and the measured deadline miss rate. The deadline miss rate is estimated using the proposed method. The difference is obtained by subtracting the estimated deadline miss rate from the measured deadline miss rate. The closer the difference is to zero, the more accurately it is estimated. The larger the difference is to a positive value, the more deadline misses in the measured than in the estimated.

First, the difference between the estimated and measured deadline miss rate is evaluated when varying the utilization of the entire DAG. The utilization is calculated based on the execution time taken by the nodes in the measurement of the actual scheduling. The utilization is classified by rounding. The y-axis represented in Fig. 6 is the percentage of the difference between the estimated and measured deadline miss rate that is more than 5%.

When comparing the estimated and measured deadline miss rates, it was found that the percentage of utilization cases where the difference exceeded 0.05 was less than 12%. Specifically, for utilization values of 0.5 and 0.625, the percentage was even lower, at less than 4%. However, as the utilization reached 0.75, the percentage of deadline miss rate differences exceeding 0.05 increased significantly.

This increase can be attributed to a higher proportion of tasks occupying the core, leading to increased waiting times for the execution of nodes in the end-to-end path. The proposed method, which does not account for waiting times, results in increased response times in actual measurements. This discrepancy between the estimated and measured response times reduces the accuracy of the estimation, leading to a higher number of observed deadline misses compared to the estimation when the core utilization reaches 0.75.

Due to the possibility of bias in the attempts, the actual measurement may vary by a few percent of the estimate. The deadline miss rate is calculated from the number of deadline misses in 200 attempts. If one deadline miss is biased, it will vary by 0.5% in this number of attempts. Considering the bias from the results of utilization 0.5 and 0.625, the proposed method can accurately estimate the number of deadline misses.

Next, the percentage difference between the estimated and measured deadline miss rate is shown when the utilization is varied. In Fig. 7, the percentage of differences in deadline miss rates of 5% or more increases as the utilization increases. In addition, the percentage with a difference of 1% or less is decreasing. As the utilization of cores increases, waiting times for node execution and the percentage of the difference above 0.05 increase. The utilization rate has a significant influence on the accuracy of the estimation of the proposed method.

The difference between the estimated and measured deadline miss rate when varying the number of timer-driven nodes is evaluated. As shown in Fig. 8, the percentage of the difference exceeding 0.1 is shown by varying the number of timer-driven nodes when the utilization is fixed at 0.75. The percentage of the difference being more than 0.1 increases until the number of timer-driven nodes increases to 14, indicating that the accuracy of the estimation is decreasing. The reason for the decrease in accuracy is that the number of nodes executing in parallel is greater than the number of cores, which creates waiting times for the nodes.

The percentage of differences between estimated and measured results of more than 0.1 was reduced when the number of timer-driven nodes varied from 14 to 16. The increased accuracy of the estimation was attributed to the utilization of chains in the end-to-end path. The utilization rate of the endto-end path chain for the number of timer-driven nodes of 16

The greater utilization of chains in the endto-end path makes it more difficult to estimate the deadline miss rate.

V. RELATED WORK Existing studies were surveyed to propose a method for the estimation of deadline misses. First, an existing study using a single-period DAG is introduced. Secondly, existing studies dealing with DAGs with multiple periods were investigated, since the autonomous-driving system has multiple timerdriven nodes. Finally, existing studies using DAG models with probabilities were surveyed. This section is a summary and comparison of these studies, which are presented in Table IV.

div.head: A. Single Rate DAG
div.p: Network-on-Chip (NoC) used for inter-core communication in many-core systems can cause conflicts. This increases timing uncertainty and makes response time estimation difficult. DAG-Order [15], a method for determining groups of tasks in which conflicts may occur and fixing the order of execution for each group, was proposed to solve this problem.

div.head: B. Multi Rate DAG
div.p: Studies dealing with a DAG with multiple periods are introduced. Heterogeneous Quasi Partitioned Scheduling (hQPS) [16] is a method aimed at reducing preemption and migration in heterogeneous multi-core systems. In addition, a study has been conducted to compute upper and lower bounds for data age under a DAG with multiple periods, considering execution time variations and release jitter [17]. Both studies target DAGs consisting only of timer-driven nodes and are used to calculate utilization and analyze dependencies from timer-driven nodes.

In the autonomous-driving system, sensors and actuators are required to deadline every period, but the processing part of the system may not be periodic. Such a system can be modeled with a Synchronous Data Flow (SDF) graph. To satisfy the periodic and node priority constraints on the SDF, an SDF scheduling method [18] has been proposed. This study allows the number of cores required to avoid deadline misses can be checked without computing a schedule.

ROS 2 [23] is used in robotic and autonomous-driving systems [1]. However, the ROS 2 executor results in behavior that deviates from standard scheduling, and conventional response time analysis methods cannot handle it. For the existing ROS 2 response time analysis that addresses this problem, an extension study [19] has been conducted to remove the parts of the system that do not execute reliably.

Autonomous-driving systems have a characteristic that node execution times and deadlines vary depending on the environment surrounding the vehicle, and this property makes it difficult to meet deadlines and optimize accuracy. To solve this problem, Dynamic Deadline-Driven (D3) [20], which unifies deadline management, was proposed. D3 receives environmental information, adjusts deadlines, and informs downstream nodes of countermeasures in the event of a deadline miss.

div.head: C. DAG Considering Probability
div.p: Studies that represent changes in the system at runtime due to conditional branches, control flow, and execution time variation of nodes with probability exist. Existing studies [13], [14] have addressed runtime changes by varying the execution time of nodes with probability. A model also exists in which the structure of the DAG itself changes probability [21]. The response time was analyzed using methods for calculating execution times and probabilities.

Trojans can harm system-on-chip (SoC) performance, and achieving a detection rate close to 100% is crucial. A method to minimize the false positive detection rate of Trojan horses while also reducing deadline misses is studied [22]. This method calculated the probability of assigning a node to a core considering deadline constraints and execution time.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we have proposed an estimation method for the deadline miss rate for each instance of a sink node in a DAG with a mixture of timer-driven and event-driven nodes. While most of the existing studies represent the execution time of a node by a single value, WCET, this study addressed the problem of the distribution of execution time for each node. The distribution of execution times was represented by a matrix of execution times and probabilities, and the response time and deadline miss rate were estimated by enumerating the dependencies among the chains that can be taken. A comparison of the deadline miss rate estimated by the proposed method and the result of scheduling showed that the proposed method accurately estimated the deadline miss rate when the number of cores was sufficient.

In future work, the proposed method can be extended to consider node interference. Currently, nodes wait for execution when no cores are available. This waiting reduces the accuracy of the deadline miss rate estimated by the proposed method. Considering node interference would increase the accuracy of the proposed method. In order to show that the proposed method is practical, the proposed method will be evaluated in a DAG for an autonomous-driving system.
